{{Short description|Property of topological spaces}}
{{Use shortened footnotes|date=December 2022}}
In [[mathematics]], a [[topological space]] is said to be '''ultraconnected''' if no two nonempty [[closed set]]s are [[disjoint (sets)|disjoint]].<ref name=PlanetMath>PlanetMath</ref> Equivalently, a space is ultraconnected if and only if the closures of two distinct points always have non trivial intersection. Hence, no [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]] with more than one point is ultraconnected.<ref name="StSe">Steen & Seebach, Sect. 4, pp. 29-30</ref>

==Properties==

Every ultraconnected space <math>X</math> is [[path-connected]] (but not necessarily [[arc connected]]).  If <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are two points of <math>X</math> and <math>p</math> is a point in the intersection <math>\operatorname{cl}\{a\}\cap\operatorname{cl}\{b\}</math>, the function <math>f:[0,1]\to X</math> defined by <math>f(t)=a</math> if <math>0 \le t < 1/2</math>, <math>f(1/2)=p</math> and <math>f(t)=b</math> if <math>1/2 < t \le 1</math>, is a continuous path between <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>.<ref name="StSe"/>

Every ultraconnected space is [[normal space|normal]], [[limit point compact]], and [[pseudocompact space|pseudocompact]].<ref name=PlanetMath/>

==Examples==

The following are examples of ultraconnected topological spaces.
* A set with the [[indiscrete topology]].
* The [[Sierpiński space]].
* A set with the [[excluded point topology]].
* The [[right order topology]] on the real line.<ref>Steen & Seebach, example #50, p. 74</ref>
